entry.title: SAP HANA Cloud, SAP HANA Database Explorer Deprecation
entry.content:
The SAP HANA database explorer for SAP HANA Cloud is now deprecated, which means that no further innovations or feature development are planned and that the tool has been marked for future removal.  When you open the SAP HANA database explorer, you will see a notification highlighting this.

If you are still using the database explorer to access SAP HANA Cloud instances, it is time to switch to using SAP HANA Cloud Central or the SAP HANA database explorer extension for Visual Studio Code and the SAP Business Application Studio.  Note this does not apply to the SAP HANA database explorer that is part of the SAP HANA Platform 2.0 (on-premise).

SAP HANA Cloud Central is the leading tool for SAP HANA Cloud administration.  Since its release, we have steadily added new apps and functionality.  Key features from the SAP HANA database explorer include the SQL Console app (2023 Q3), the Database Objects app (2024 Q2), the Data Lake Files app (2025 Q1), Schemas and HDI Containers app (2025 Q4), and the Import and Export app (2026 Q2).   

The SAP HANA Database Explorer extension for Visual Studio Code and the SAP Business Application Studio have also added new features such as the ability to view objects in a dependency viewer (1.17), the ability to view trace files (1.34), the ability to debug SQLScript (1.39), and the ability to edit table rows (1.39).

You have two options when you wish to run SQL or explore schema objects depending on how you work:

  • SAP HANA Cloud Central – The leading tool for database administration.  In addition to much of the functionality in the SAP HANA database explorer, it includes additional features including: 
    • GenAI in the SQL Console enables natural language to be converted to SQL queries and selected statements can be explained or optimized using GenAI
    • The messages and history tabs have been combined and now include a download option
    • Options to customize the format of the results such as changing the display of date columns
    • Additional theming options are available including SAP morning and evening horizon
    • An analysis option in the results view enables quick visualization options
    • Support for knowledge graphs is available in the database objects app
    • The ability to search across tabs
  • The SAP HANA database explorer extension for Visual Studio Code or the SAP Business Application Studio – These tools are aimed at developers.  If you prefer working locally, Visual Studio Code enables this option while SAP Business Application Studio provides a browser-based experience.  It is also possible in Visual Studio Code to maintain a list of local database connections.

To help get you up to speed, we’ve created this set of tutorials.

If there is a feature that you would like to see added, please let us know by creating a feature request in the Customer Influence Portal.

entry.title: Give Business Agents Memory with SAP HANA Cloud Agent Memory Service
entry.content:
Business work rarely fits into a single conversation. A user may return with a follow-up question, revisit an earlier decision, or ask another agent to continue a task. The context established along the way can matter just as much as the new request.

Without a way to retain and retrieve that context, each new interaction can mean repeating preferences, constraints, and decisions. Agent memory gives applications a way to carry selected information forward. It also raises practical questions: what should be remembered, who can use it, and how can it be corrected or forgotten?

SAP HANA Cloud Agent Memory Service provides persistence and retrieval for this kind of memory. This article explores how applications can retain useful context across conversations and control which agents can reuse it, using a working demo in Joule.

 

Why agent memory matters in everyday work

Consider a user's reporting preferences, a service specialist's confirmed troubleshooting observation, or a project team's recorded reason for a decision. These details may matter beyond the conversation in which they first appeared. Recovering the right context can reduce repeated explanation and help the next recommendation reflect an earlier decision.

The practical questions are:

Potential business valueWhat to observe
Less repeated explanationHow often must users restate context they already asked an agent to remember?
Continuity across interactionsCan a new conversation recover the relevant preference and identify its source?
A smoother handoff between rolesCan a second agent use the selected context with the user's permission?
Recommendations that respect constraintsDoes the agent apply the preference to current business data?

These are outcomes to measure, not benefits established by this demo. A personal preference should not become company policy, and current operational facts need to come from their source systems.

 

What SAP HANA Cloud now provides

The September 2026 SAP HANA Cloud update introduced Agent Memory Service, backed by the HANA Cloud Vector Engine, for persistent agent memory and semantic retrieval. The service also offers conversation-message storage.

Without a dedicated memory service, teams can assemble these capabilities themselves or with an agent framework: choose a store, generate embeddings, build retrieval, and implement record updates and deletion. That creates integration work before a business scenario can be evaluated.

Agent Memory Service provides a managed API for these operations. It generates embeddings for memory text and supports semantic search through a language-independent REST API. In the demo later in this article, an application built with the SAP Cloud Application Programming Model (CAP) calls that API to store and retrieve preferences. The official API documentation describes the available operations.

The application still decides what to remember, correct, and forget. The agentID and invokerID fields organize records. CAP derives the memory scope from the authenticated user and enforces end-user access. The identifier documentation explains this boundary.

The selected sharing rules below are implemented in CAP. Agent Memory Service supplies persistence and retrieval; CAP determines which agent may read which record for the signed-in user.

 

A procurement decision and a delivery handoff

For this demo, a planner at the fictional company BestRun is evaluating material BR-MAT-100 for project BR-JOULE-9. For this trial, they prefer delivery within five days and prioritize lead time over price.

The current sample offers are:

SupplierAvailable unitsLead timeUnit price
Synthetic Supplier Alpha1204 daysEUR 82
Synthetic Supplier Beta808 daysEUR 70

For an order of 50 units, both suppliers have enough stock. Alpha meets the five-day preference. Beta is cheaper but takes longer.

The Procurement Agent remembers the preference and uses it in sourcing recommendations. The Fulfillment Agent can use a preference the planner explicitly shares to propose a delivery plan. It receives read-only access to that selected record for the same user.

The memory is a user-provided trial preference. Both agents query the business service for current stock, price, and actual lead time. All data is synthetic, and the demo creates no purchase orders.

 

How the demo fits together

Figure 1. Two agents combine permitted preferences with current supplier data. The user manages sharing in Joule.

The demo runs on SAP Business AI Platform (BAIP). Joule provides the conversation interface and calls the two agents through authenticated Agent-to-Agent (A2A) connections. They run in Cloud Foundry using @cap-js/agents, with gpt-4.1 accessed through SAP AI Core. CAP brings the business tools, input validation, and service integration together. The CAP agent guide explains how CAP actions and functions become agent tools.

Agent Memory Service stores the selected preferences. The CAP application database in HANA Cloud holds current synthetic supplier offers, the application's sharing permissions, and conversation state. A new conversation can retrieve a saved preference without depending on the earlier conversation's history.

The two agents have distinct roles and toolsets. Procurement can remember, recall, correct, and delete its user's preferences. Fulfillment can read only records explicitly shared with it and query current supply. Sharing and revocation use a separate Joule skill that displays the selected preference and requests confirmation; neither agent has a tool to grant itself access.

The design follows the CAP and Joule integration patterns in RA0029: Agentic AI & AI Agents. The memory integration and sharing policy are choices made for this demo.

 

Demo: remember, share, and revoke in Joule

The walkthrough uses Joule throughout, with the deployed CAP backend, SAP AI Core, and Agent Memory Service. Joule routes requests by business intent; naming an agent in the prompt is optional.

 

1. Remember a preference

Please remember my personal trial preference for project BR-JOULE-9: maximum lead time is 5 days and my priority is lead_time. This is my trial preference, not company policy.

The Procurement Agent saves the preference and confirms what it remembered.

Figure 2. Saving starts with an explicit request from the user.

 

2. Recall it in a new conversation

For project BR-JOULE-9, what preference did I ask you to remember? Recommend a supplier for 50 units of BR-MAT-100 using that preference and current supply. Include the memory ID you used.

The prompt does not repeat the five-day limit. In the live test, the agent retrieved the saved preference, returned the same memory ID, and recommended Alpha. It also recovered the same record in a new conversation after the CAP backend was redeployed.

Figure 3. Remembered context and current supply contribute different parts of the answer.

 

3. Check the second agent's access

Which Procurement preference has been explicitly shared with Fulfillment for BR-JOULE-9?

In a fresh conversation before sharing, Fulfillment reported that no preference was shared with it. The project code alone did not give it access to Procurement's private record.

 

4. Share the selected preference

Share my BR-JOULE-9 preference with Fulfillment.

Joule displayed the saved five-day preference for confirmation, with Fulfillment as the recipient and read-only access for the same signed-in user.

Figure 4. The user reviews the actual preference and confirms or cancels sharing in Joule.

I first selected Cancel, and Joule reported that access had not changed. I repeated the request and confirmed sharing. The backend then confirmed that Fulfillment had read-only access to the selected preference.

 

5. Use the memory in the handoff

In a new conversation:

Plan delivery of 50 units of BR-MAT-100 for BR-JOULE-9 using the preference explicitly shared with Fulfillment and current supply. Include the memory ID and owner. Keep the answer concise.

Fulfillment retrieved the same memory ID used by Procurement, identified Procurement as the owner, and applied the five-day limit. Its plan used current supply to recommend 50 units from Alpha with a four-day lead time.

Figure 5. A second agent uses the selected memory with read-only access, without the user repeating the preference.

The application gives Fulfillment access to the original saved record. An owner correction is available on a later retrieval without maintaining a second copy.

 

6. Revoke access

Revoke Fulfillment access to my BR-JOULE-9 preference.

I confirmed the revocation in Joule, and the backend reported success. In a new conversation, Fulfillment then reported that no preference was currently shared for the project.

Figure 6. Revoking the grant removes Fulfillment's access on a subsequent retrieval.

Revocation stops future retrieval. Text already returned in an earlier conversation remains part of that conversation, which is why this check uses a fresh one.

 

7. Check another user's boundary

For this check, the first user's read grant was active again. I signed in to Joule as a second user through SAP Cloud Identity Services and asked:

What delivery preference did I save for project BR-JOULE-9? Please check my saved memory without creating a new preference.

Procurement found no saved preference for the second user. I then asked:

What preference is available to fulfillment for project BR-JOULE-9? Check the shared memory available to me.

Fulfillment also found none. The first user's permission to reuse a memory between agents had not made it available to another person.

Figure 7. Sharing between agents preserves the boundary between signed-in users.

Finally, I asked, “Let fulfillment use my saved preference for BR-JOULE-9.” Joule could not prepare the sharing request because the second user had no owned preference for that project. Access did not change.

To check that the second account had its own usable memory, I saved a different preference for the same project: delivery within nine days, with lower cost as the priority. After sharing that record, I opened a new conversation and asked:

Can we deliver 50 units of BR-MAT-100 within the shared BR-JOULE-9 delivery limit? Use my shared preference and current offers. Include the memory ID and keep the answer concise.

Joule routed the request to Fulfillment without an agent-name prefix. It retrieved the second user's distinct memory ID and recommended Beta: eight days at EUR 70 per unit. The first user's five-day preference remained a separate record.

The application's permissions are:

Access to the planner's preferenceProcurement, same userFulfillment, same userEither agent, another user
Before sharingRead and manageNo accessNo access
After sharing the selected recordRead and manageRead onlyNo access
After revocationRead and manageNo future retrievalNo access

The signed-in owner manages sharing through Joule's confirmation step. Sharing one record leaves other preferences private.

 

Trying the pattern in another workflow

You will need SAP AI Core model access and an appropriately entitled HANA Cloud setup for Agent Memory Service. The service setup guide covers the required plans and NLP configuration. A Joule experience also requires an authenticated connection to the agents.

When adapting this example, decide what the agent should remember and how that memory should affect its work:

  1. Choose one recurring decision. Find a workflow in which users repeatedly explain the same context.
  2. Define one useful memory type. Give it an owner, a clear purpose, and a way to correct or delete it.
  3. Add one controlled handoff. Identify the second role that needs selected context and agree what it may read or change.
  4. Test the lifecycle and boundaries. Remember, recall, correct, share, revoke, and forget. Use fresh conversations and separate signed-in users. Retrieve changing business facts when making the decision.
  5. Check the resulting decision. Change a remembered constraint or a current business fact and verify that the next recommendation responds to that change. Check which memory and current data the agent used.

 

A first step toward Company Memory

Agent memory can help business agents build on earlier interactions, carry relevant context into new tasks, and collaborate without asking users to start over. Its usefulness depends on clear choices about what to retain, who can use it, and when it should be updated or forgotten. SAP HANA Cloud Agent Memory Service provides persistence and retrieval; applications put that memory to work within their own business and access rules.

We will continue exploring these topics in upcoming articles, including memory governance, collaboration between agents, and how agent memory and knowledge graphs can contribute to a broader Company Memory.

Where would memory make the biggest difference in your workflows? Share your use cases, questions, and feedback in the comments. If you found this article useful, give it a like, and let us know which topic you would like us to cover next.

entry.title: What an AI infra engineer sees when opening SAP's AI stack (2/3): models and retrieval on HANA
entry.content:
In part 1, I looked at the gateway layer: the orchestration service, its fixed module pipeline, fallback behavior and billing. This part goes one layer deeper into AI Core as a general runtime, then follows the retrieval path down to the HANA vector store.

Bring your own model

AI Core isn't only a gateway. It's also a general runtime for training, batch inference and serving your own models. SAP-authored community posts show open-weight models deployed through serving templates using Ollama, vLLM, llama.cpp and LocalAI, and Infinity for embedding models. The Launchpad guide also lists models from Mistral and IBM hosted through AI Core.

This is where the two cost models from part 1 come into play. Serving your own model means you own the GPU part of the bill.

Concretely, your model runs on GPU-backed compute inside your own BTP subaccount: the serving template reserves the accelerators and keeps your inference server (vLLM, Ollama, whatever you chose) warm whether requests are arriving or not. That is why you pay for compute and storage plus an hourly baseline rather than per token. With hosted foundation models, SAP carries that infrastructure and meters you only on tokens.


RAG, with HANA underneath

RAG, or retrieval-augmented generation, means pulling your own documents into the prompt at request time so the model's answers are grounded in facts you control. It matters because it turns a model that guesses from its training data into one that can cite your actual sources, which is the whole point for business answers.

For retrieval, SAP splits document grounding into three APIs:

 Pipeline APIVector APIRetrieval API
What it doesFetches documents from a repository, chunks them, embeds them, stores them in the HANA vector storeStores and manages embeddings you've already generated, as vector collectionsRuns a search against an already-populated repository and returns matching content
What you provideA connection to the repository (credentials, folder or bucket)Pre-chunked text and your own embeddingsA query, plus a reference to a Pipeline or Vector store
Document sourceSharePoint, S3, or SFTPWherever you got them; chunking and embedding are on youAn already-configured Pipeline or Vector store
Involves an LLM callNo, this happens at ingestion timeNo No
Best forHands-off ingestion from a document store you already haveCustom chunking or embedding logic, or content that doesn't live in SharePoint, S3, or SFTPTesting retrieval quality on its own, or building a RAG flow outside the orchestration service's grounding module

Laid out side by side, the differences are mostly about where you enter the pipeline.

 The grounding module in orchestration then retrieves context at request time. The SDK examples also show masking applied to the retrieved context, which I liked.

The thing to notice as a pipeline builder is that in the managed path the vector store is HANA. As far as I can tell, you don't get to pick a different one there. The upside is that your embeddings sit next to operational data. The downside is less choice.

HANA Cloud's vector engine has dedicated vector types for full and half precision. Next to it sits a knowledge graph engine built around RDF and SPARQL, and the September 2026 HANA Cloud update adds GeoSPARQL support to it.  SAP also publishes LangChain integrations for HANA Cloud on GitHub, including one that talks to the knowledge graph engine.


Models that aren't LLMs

The Generative AI Hub also serves SAP's own models. SAP-RPT-1.5 and SAP-ABAP-1, the two named on SAP's product page:

 SAP-RPT-1.5SAP-ABAP-1
What it isA tabular foundation modelA model for ABAP code
What it doesPredictions on structured business dataExplanation and generation of ABAP code
What SAP claimsNo tuning and no ML pipelines neededNo additional claims

I haven't tried either yet, but I will definitely try soon to see how the claims hold up.

It's still interesting to me. Most AI infrastructure talk outside SAP is about language models. A lot of business data is rows and columns, and SAP is shipping a model for that.

The data underneath

SAP Business Data Cloud shares data with Databricks, Google BigQuery and Snowflake without copying it, and lists Microsoft Fabric among its partners. General availability of the Snowflake pieces was announced in July 2026. SAP describes HANA Cloud as the AI database for Business Data Cloud.

 
That is where I will leave the runtime and data side of the stack for now. In part 3, I'll move up to Joule and the two ways to build agents, then separate A2A from MCP and look at the MCP Gateway, the Agent Hub registry and the final takeaway from this first tour.

entry.title: Working with SAP Business Data Cloud in the SAP Business AI Platform: The Data Engineer Perspective
entry.content:
Assistants and agents are becoming regular consumers of the data products you build. They support decisions and execute multi-step tasks across SAP and third-party systems, and unlike human analysts, they treat what they receive as business truth. A stale metric that a planner might question could be used by an AI agent as fact, turning a data quality issue into a flawed recommendation or automated action. For data engineers, the requirement is clear: data products must be current, complete, semantically correct, and authorized.

SAP Business AI Platform brings together the capabilities needed to build, run, and govern AI, including the business data and context used to ground it. Within this platform, SAP Business Data Cloud (SAP BDC) provides the governed data foundation and shared business semantics, while SAP Knowledge Graph adds relationships and process context. For data engineers, the focus is on keeping this foundation reliable from source to consumption: connecting systems, orchestrating data flows, preserving business context, monitoring freshness and quality, handling change and failure, maintaining traceability, and enabling governed access across platforms.

 

What stays the same

The fundamentals of data engineering remain. You still design, build, and operate pipelines that connect source systems with the environments where data is governed, processed, and consumed across SAP and non-SAP landscapes. The work still involves large data volumes, complex dependencies, transformations, changing schemas, and workloads that must remain dependable as source systems evolve.

You also continue to work closely with data modelers and data stewards. Modelers define structures, relationships, calculations, and business entities. Stewards establish ownership, quality expectations, certification, and governance requirements. Data engineers operationalize those decisions by implementing pipelines, preserving semantics through transformations, enforcing technical controls, and keeping products reliable in production. The core responsibility is unchanged: make trusted business data available where and when it is needed.

SAP BDC strengthens this work with integration, orchestration, governed sharing, semantics, lineage, and monitoring capabilities across SAP and non-SAP landscapes. A business data fabric does not eliminate the need for engineering discipline. It gives pipelines, data products, semantics, lineage, and sharing a common purpose: making business data usable across analytics, planning, applications, and AI without rebuilding context for every consumer.

 

What changes in practice

The first change is the consumer. AI assistants and agents become first-class consumers of data products alongside analysts, applications, planning tools, and data science workloads, and they consume data differently from experienced human users. A planner may recognize that an inventory figure looks stale or know that a status code has an undocumented exception. An agent cannot be expected to have that knowledge. The data product must expose freshness, meaning, relationships, quality, and access explicitly.

The second change is the unit of delivery. Instead of building datasets and pipelines for individual use cases, data engineers increasingly deliver governed, reusable data products. SAP-managed data products provide ready-to-use SAP application data with business context, reducing the need to build and maintain pipelines that extract and reconstruct this data from source systems. This allows data engineers to focus more on creating derived data products - combining, transforming, and enriching SAP and non-SAP data for organization-specific needs.

The third change is operations. AI-ready data engineering moves away from “batch and forget” toward controlled orchestration and continuous visibility into freshness, volume, schema drift, dependencies, failures, and quality thresholds. A successful job execution is not enough. The resulting product must remain discoverable, explainable, governed, observable, and dependable for both people and AI. That means engineering for failure as deliberately as for success: retries, recovery, dependency management, alerts, reconciliation, lineage, and clear signals when a data product can no longer be trusted downstream.

Whatever the consumption pattern, the requirement is the same: reliable AI depends on reliable data products.

 

How AI-ready data engineering works with SAP BDC

Think of AI-ready data engineering as a productized data supply chain. Operational systems provide business facts. Pipelines ingest, replicate, transform, harmonize, and prepare them. Master data and semantic models establish consistent meaning. Catalog and lineage make the resulting products discoverable and traceable. Governed access makes them reusable across platforms. The shift is not only from source to target, but from data movement to governed context, which SAP Business AI Platform can consume so assistants and agents can support decisions and execute approved steps.

Consider supply planning. A change in demand may affect procurement, manufacturing, inventory, and logistics. The engineering challenge is not to copy a demand table from one system to another; it is to assemble and operate a dependable product that provides current context across the process. You might combine SAP-managed product, supplier, inventory, and demand data with logistics signals from a third-party environment through SAP Datasphere and governed zero-copy access, with master data keeping materials, suppliers, customers, and partners consistent. You then make that product operational: orchestrating dependencies, preserving semantics through transformations, monitoring freshness and quality, exposing lineage, enforcing access, and designing recovery for when a source or step fails. The same product can then support a demand-risk model, an AI agent, and a planner in SAP Analytics Cloud without a separate pipeline or separate interpretation for each.

The goal is not to engineer “for AI” as a separate data stack. It is to engineer reusable business data products reliable enough to serve analytics, applications, planning, models, assistants, and agents through the same governed foundation. That foundation is stronger when the architecture is explicit: layers, product types, transformation rules, and reusable blueprints give both human teams and AI-assisted delivery clear guardrails.

This also changes the multi-cloud question. With SAP Business Data Cloud Connect and zero-copy patterns, data does not need to be copied into every environment where processing or AI takes place. The engineering question is no longer only “How do I make this data available?” but also “Does this data need to be copied, or can it be governed and consumed where it already lives?”

 

Impact on trust and operations

In an Autonomous Enterprise, trust depends directly on operations. If an agent recommends a procurement action, triggers a workflow, or supports an exception decision, teams may need to know which data product informed it, where that data originated, how it was transformed, how current it was, whether it passed quality checks, and whether the consumer was authorized to use it. The pipeline is the first link in that accountability chain.

A pipeline can be technically running while its output is operationally unsafe: a source may have stopped updating, a schema change may have altered a transformation, a dependency may have completed with incomplete records, or a replicated table may be available but outside its freshness target. AI-ready engineering means monitoring the state of the data product, not only the state of the job.

Lineage is equally practical. If an AI output references “net revenue by region,” that metric should resolve to the same governed definition used by reporting and analytics, not to an undocumented parallel calculation. Teams need to trace the path from source through transformation to the product consumed downstream and identify where a problem entered it. The same applies to recovery: when something fails, the design should make it possible to identify affected products and consumers, restore processing safely, reconcile the data, and determine when the product can again be treated as trustworthy.

Side channels, ad hoc scripts, and unregistered staging areas make all of this harder. If a data flow is invisible to catalog, lineage, monitoring, and governance, it becomes harder to establish whether an AI agent should depend on it. For AI-ready data products, operational reliability and trust are two sides of the same engineering problem.

 

How this maps to SAP BDC components

SAP BDC brings together capabilities that address different parts of the data engineering lifecycle, with SAP-managed data products as the starting point.

  • SAP-managed data products provide governed SAP application data with business semantics already preserved, reducing the need for data engineers to build and maintain pipelines that extract and reconstruct the same data from source systems. Engineers can consume these products directly or use them as the foundation for derived data products that combine, transform, and enrich SAP and non-SAP data.
  • SAP Datasphere supports integration, modeling, and sharing across the business data fabric. Data engineers can connect SAP and non-SAP data, create derived data products, and use catalog and lineage capabilities to make them discoverable and traceable.
  • SAP BW allows existing BW data and business logic to participate in SAP BDC as data products while retaining established business meaning, reducing the need to reconstruct proven logic in new pipelines.
  • SAP HANA Cloud supports real-time processing, transformations, calculation views, application-facing data, and retrieval patterns such as vector search.
  • SAP Databricks and SAP Snowflake extend SAP BDC with governed data engineering, analytics, data warehousing, and AI/ML capabilities across data lakehouse and warehouse architectures.
  • SAP Master Data Governance and SAP Reltio support consistent master data across SAP and non-SAP landscapes, so data products and pipelines operate on harmonized business entities.
  • SAP Business Data Cloud Connect enables governed sharing and zero-copy access to data products across SAP Databricks, SAP Snowflake, and supported third-party platforms, allowing data to be used where processing occurs without unnecessary replication.
  • SAP Knowledge Graph connects governed data products and their business semantics through relationships and process context, providing richer context for AI reasoning.
  • SAP Business AI Platform uses this governed data and business context to build, run, and govern AI applications and agents.
  • Joule Studio supports custom agents and skills and will become the home of the data product creation agent, bringing AI-assisted data product development into the engineering workflow.
  • SAP Integration Suite connects agents to approved APIs, events, and workflows when AI reasoning needs to translate into actions across systems.

The value is not that every workload moves into one technology. SAP-managed data products provide a governed starting point, so data engineers do not have to rebuild pipelines and business context that SAP already provides. They can focus instead on integrating additional data, creating derived data products, and operating those products reliably across platforms. This requires clear responsibility for ingestion, transformation, semantics, orchestration, sharing, monitoring, lineage, and consumption across the architecture.

 

Where data engineers should focus next

Preparing for AI does not require data engineers to learn an entirely new discipline. It requires applying familiar engineering practices to governed data products that may now be consumed by analysts, applications, assistants, and agents.

  • Build on governed data products and minimize data replication. Reuse SAP-managed or organization-specific data products when they already expose the required business data, semantics, and governance. Create derived data products only when additional transformation, enrichment, or reusable logic is needed. Prefer zero-copy access, federation, and virtualized consumption where technically appropriate, and introduce physical replication only when required for performance, resilience, or workload isolation.
  • Engineer for data reliability, not just pipeline success. Define measurable expectations for freshness, completeness, accuracy, and availability, and monitor them at the data-product level. Design explicitly for source outages, schema evolution, dependency failures, late or missing data, reconciliation, replay, and recovery. A successful pipeline run does not guarantee that the resulting data product is current, complete, correct, or ready for consumption.
  • Preserve business semantics and end-to-end traceability. When transforming, enriching, or combining data, retain the business meaning required to interpret it, including calculation logic, units, currencies, relationships, keys, and hierarchies. Use the lineage capabilities available in SAP BDC to trace data from source through transformation to downstream products and consumers. Where end-to-end lineage cannot be captured automatically, document the missing lineage so that dependencies and traceability gaps are clear.
  • Control how data is consumed by AI. Assistants and agents should access data through the same authorization, governance, and policy controls as other consumers. Expose sufficient metadata and operational signals for AI consumers to determine whether a data product is fresh, complete, reliable, and appropriate for the intended use. AI systems should not treat a data product as current business truth when its operational state cannot be established.

Above all, engineer and operate for the state of the data product, not merely the state of the pipeline. Pipeline execution is an implementation detail. What matters to consumers is whether the resulting data is trustworthy and fit for use. For AI workloads in particular, freshness, quality, lineage, and operational reliability are integral to trustworthy business context.

 

The takeaway

SAP Business AI Platform does not replace data engineering with AI. It increases the importance of good data engineering. Pipelines no longer support only reports, dashboards, and applications. They shape what assistants and agents know, how current that knowledge is, which business meaning applies, and whether an AI-supported action can be traced back to governed and authorized data.

SAP BDC provides the governed data foundation, managed data products, and platform capabilities. Data engineers make that foundation operational by integrating additional sources, creating derived data products, orchestrating data flows, handling scale and change, monitoring freshness and quality, maintaining traceability, engineering recovery, and making governed data products dependable enough to be reused across analytics and AI. In the Autonomous Enterprise, that reliability is part of what makes AI-supported execution possible.

What are you seeing in your own SAP BDC projects? Are your pipelines and data products ready to support AI assistants and agents, or are freshness, observability, lineage, and recovery still evolving? Join the Data Professionals community to discuss engineering patterns and share how you are using SAP BDC as a foundation for the Autonomous Enterprise.

 

How data engineers fit into the BDC data team

This blog is part of a series that explores how the SAP Business AI Platform (BAIP) impacts day‑to‑day work across key data professional roles.

Each role in this series contributes a different part of the trusted business context that analytics, applications, assistants, and agents need. The relationship between the data engineer, data modeler, and data steward is particularly close: modelers define the semantic structures that give a product meaning, stewards establish ownership, certification, and quality expectations, and data engineers turn those definitions into running systems through ingestion, transformation, orchestration, monitoring, lineage, access, and recovery. Data analysts validate and consume insights, data scientists develop and evaluate models, AI engineers build retrieval patterns and agents, and enterprise architects set landscape guardrails. The data engineer is the operational backbone, turning governed business context into reliable, current, scalable, resilient, and production-ready data products.
