entry.title: SAP HANA Cloud Expands Availability on SAP Sovereign Cloud — What It Means for Regulated Customers
entry.content:
In the September 2026 edition of What’s New in SAP HANA Cloud, we announced availability in two new SAP Sovereign Cloud regions, released during the Q3 2026 timeframe. With this expansion, SAP HANA Cloud is now available across the Five-Eyes countries, Europe/Germany, and India, addressing customer demand for digital sovereignty in additional geographies.

SAP HANA Cloud availability on SAP Sovereign Cloud and SAP NS2

 

This blog highlights two significant milestones: the new availability in Europe/Germany and the new FedRAMP certification at SAP NS2 in the United States with SAP NS2. 

Now Available to Highly Regulated European Customers

Europe/Germany is the first deployment of SAP Sovereign Cloud in Europe. It brings SAP’s sovereign solutions to organizations with elevated regulatory and security requirements — those that typically cannot adopt SAP’s public cloud offering. SAP HANA Cloud is among the solutions available in this landscape at launch.

A Fully Sovereign, SAP-Owned Foundation

The Europe/Germany deployment runs on SAP Cloud Infrastructure, an Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS) platform developed by SAP and based on open-source technologies. By owning and operating every layer — from infrastructure to application — SAP enables sovereignty across the full technology stack.

Key characteristics include:

  • Independent from third-party cloud providers: The environment runs on SAP’s own infrastructure.
  • A sovereign region of SAP Cloud Infrastructure: The region is hosted in SAP-owned data centers in Walldorf and St. Leon-Rot. In June 2026, SAP received Authorization to Use from the German Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) to process information classified as VS-NfD ("Restricted — For Official Use Only") on SAP Cloud Infrastructure in these data centers.
  • Data residency in Germany: All data, including telemetry, remains in Germany.
  • Local operations: Administration and maintenance are handled by security-cleared personnel based in Germany.
  • A locally hosted control plane: The control plane remains within the region, supporting technical sovereignty.
  • A European legal entity: The service is provided by SAP SE.

Together, these characteristics give highly regulated European organizations a way to adopt SAP HANA Cloud while meeting their sovereignty, security, and compliance requirements.

Now Ready for Adoption by U.S. Federal Civilian Agencies

SAP HANA Cloud at SAP NS2 has achieved FedRAMP Moderate certification and is now available to U.S. federal civilian agencies through the SAP NS2 Government Cloud.

This U.S.-based cloud environment, delivered by SAP NS2,  meets stringent U.S. security and compliance requirements. It runs on AWS GovCloud, is managed exclusively by U.S. citizens, and all operations and data are restricted to U.S. soil.

SAP HANA Cloud has been generally available at SAP NS2 since 2025, serving commercial customers in regulated industries, such as Defense Industrial Base (DIB) and utility providers. The FedRAMP certification now extends access to U.S. federal civilian agencies seeking to build secure, compliant, data-driven applications.

Learn more about SAP HANA Cloud at SAP NS2.

What This Means for Customers

For highly regulated enterprises and public sector organizations, these milestones help address a long-standing trade-off between cloud innovation and digital sovereignty. Whether running on SAP Sovereign Cloud in Europe, or in the FedRAMP-certified SAP NS2 environment in the U.S., customers can process their sensitive data and analytics workloads in sovereign settings — with control across the data, operational, technical, and legal dimensions — while benefiting from the in-memory speed, elastic cloud scalability, and continuous innovation of SAP HANA Cloud.

--

Thanks to Marc Ng from SAP and Joshua Kuhn, Ashley Jennings, and Ayveri Lane from SAP NS2 for reviewing this post.

entry.title: SAP TechEd 2026: Must-Attend Sessions for Data Professionals
entry.content:
SAP TechEd 2026 (October 27–29) offers no shortage of sessions on data, AI, architecture, and analytics. The harder question is which ones deserve a place on your agenda. With SAP Business Data Cloud now in production and AI capabilities expanding across the SAP portfolio, this year’s most valuable sessions should help you, the practitioner, move beyond product updates to make better decisions about what to build, govern, modernize, and scale.

This blog narrows the field to the sessions I believe are most relevant for five data and AI practitioner personas: Enterprise Architects, Data Stewards, Data Engineers, Data Analysts, and Data Scientists. The selections emphasize practical takeaways, from designing governed data foundations and modernizing pipelines to enabling trusted, context-rich AI, so you can focus on the sessions most likely to inform your next project.

Whether attending in-person or virtual start building your agenda now — choose the sessions that match your role and share your must-attend picks with peers in the Data and AI Professionals community to keep the conversation and practical learning going well beyond the event.

This list reflects my own picks, so I've likely missed a few gems. If there's a session you're planning to attend that didn't make the cut, drop it in the comments — I'd love to know what's on your radar.

 

Keynotes

KEY100 | Built for the ones who build

KEY100V | Built for the ones who build (virtual)

Why Attend

SAP TechEd's opening keynote answers the question every architect and practitioner is asking: what can I actually build on SAP's AI platform today? SAP unifies AI, business data, governance, agents, and a new UX layer into one integrated platform — eliminating manual data pipelines, model training overhead, and unpredictable AI costs. Hear directly from SAP leadership what is production-ready now and leave with a clear picture of the business outcomes you can start delivering immediately.

Key Takeaways

  • SAP Business AI Platform unifies AI, data, governance, agents, and UX into one platform — eliminating manual pipeline setup, training overhead, and unpredictable infrastructure costs.
  • Designed so developers, architects, and practitioners focus on building outcomes, not managing underlying complexity.
  • For IT leaders evaluating adoption timelines, this session defines what is production-ready now versus what is on the horizon.

 

KEY101 | Agent v0.0.7 - A license to skill

KEY101V | Agent v0.0.7 - A license to skill (virtual)

Why Attend

Master the AI-driven development revolution. Join Agent Kasimir to see how SAP Business AI Platform, Joule Studio, and open ecosystem tools empower practitioners in AI-driven development. The session shows data professionals how agentic orchestration and context-aware AI work together — redefining how enterprise solutions are built across SAP and non-SAP environments. Evaluating how AI agents fit your analytics workflows? This session moves you from concept to action.

Key Takeaways

  • Joule Studio gives practitioners a supported entry point to build and orchestrate enterprise-grounded AI agents — without starting from scratch.
  • Data professionals get a path to AI workflows where agents reason over business data, coordinate, and integrate across SAP and non-SAP tools.
  • SAP's agentic AI is built on openness — ecosystem tools sit first-class alongside SAP-native capabilities, amplifying existing investments, not displacing them.

 

Enterprise Architects

ST135 | Agent interoperability: Protocols, patterns, and enterprise strategy

Why Attend

As multi-agent AI reaches enterprise scale, interoperability becomes an architectural imperative — this strategy session delivers the protocol-level knowledge architects and developers need. It covers open standards and integration patterns, including A2A and MCP, enabling secure, composable agent networks across SAP and third-party platforms. Leave with the foundation for enterprise-scale AI architectures designed to interoperate — not just orchestrate.

Key Takeaways

  • Agent2Agent (A2A) defines how AI agents from different vendors communicate — the foundational protocol for multi-agent networks spanning SAP and third-party systems.
  • MCP governs agent access to enterprise tools and APIs — mastering A2A and MCP together is essential for reliable cross-platform architectures at enterprise scale.
  • The session delivers practical patterns for building secure, composable agent networks across SAP and non-SAP — a blueprint for expanding agent ecosystems confidently.

 

XP113 | Build AI agents on SAP and non-SAP data and context in an open lakehouse

Why Attend

If your organization is evaluating SAP Business Data Cloud with Dremio, this is the technical blueprint for building AI agents that reason across your full data estate without siloed or ungoverned copies. The session shows how architects and developers use Apache Iceberg and Apache Polaris to integrate SAP and third-party data in an open lakehouse — creating governed data products and ontologies that power Joule agents and enable external consumption through A2A. You'll leave with a clear, end-to-end path from unified data to production-ready agentic AI.

Key Takeaways

  • An open lakehouse on Apache Iceberg and Apache Polaris unifies SAP and third-party data into a single governed layer — giving AI agents real-time access to the full data estate without movement, duplication, or governance compromise.
  • Zero-copy access ensures AI agents always reason over current, authoritative data — reducing management overhead while keeping security and compliance controls intact.
  • A2A protocols extend governed data products beyond SAP boundaries — giving architects a composable foundation where Joule and third-party agents access business context through standardized, controlled interfaces.

 

RA110 | Joule and SAP Knowledge Graph: Context-aware AI across SAP solutions

RA110V | Joule and SAP Knowledge Graph: Context-aware AI across SAP solutions (virtual)

Why Attend

Context separates a generically intelligent AI from one that truly understands your business — this session reveals how SAP AI Core, the orchestration layer behind Joule, delivers that context at scale. You’ll learn how to extend Joule Agents, leverage the Joule Studio model library, connect SAP Business Data Cloud data products, and embed AI directly in SAP S/4HANA. For professionals designing AI agent architectures or SAP analytics integrations, this is where governance, context, and intelligence converge in a production-ready architecture.

Key Takeaways

  • SAP AI Core is the orchestration layer that governs how Joule agents access models, coordinate reasoning, and embed AI directly into SAP S/4HANA within a fully auditable architecture.
  • Joule agents ground every action in trusted data via SAP Business Data Cloud and AI Core, while SAP Knowledge Graph anchors reasoning in real business relationships — delivering business-aware decisions, not generic predictions.
  • The result is an AI architecture where context, governance, and intelligence are built in by design — giving architects a production-ready foundation for extending Joule across analytics, planning, and S/4HANA use cases.

 

Data Stewards

ST200 | The next evolution of SAP Business Data Cloud with Dremio and SAP Reltio

Why Attend

SAP’s 2026 acquisitions of Dremio and Reltio are reshaping Business Data Cloud’s data fabric — this session gives architects and stewards the full picture on governance, master data quality, and the trusted foundation agentic AI requires — and what your organization needs to act on now.

Key Takeaways

  • Dremio’s Iceberg-native integration extends Business Data Cloud into an enterprise lakehouse — giving AI agents zero-copy access to current, authoritative SAP and non-SAP data while preserving governance.
  • SAP Reltio delivers AI-native MDM to Business Data Cloud — harmonizing trusted golden records across data domains so agents have the consistent reference layer they need to reason reliably in production.
  • Together, Dremio and Reltio close enterprise AI’s two critical gaps — unified data access without duplication, and trusted master data quality — delivering the governed foundation agentic AI demands at scale.

 

XP826 | Get a road map to your data products foundation: Powering AI outcomes

Why Attend

AI agents deliver value only when they know what data exists, where it lives, and whether it can be trusted. This session gives architects and stewards a practical road map for integrating governance, quality, and context to make enterprise data AI-ready — so agents can query the right information at scale to drive measurable outcomes.

Key Takeaways

  • Trusted data foundations require ongoing discipline — governance, quality, and semantic context at every layer so agents can discover, assess, and act with confidence.
  • Governance, quality, and context must travel with the data — keeping agents within defined trust boundaries wherever data resides.
  • Data products — governed, reusable, context-enriched units — are the building block for scaling AI outcomes, letting multiple agents consume trusted data without duplicating governance effort.

 

DA104 | Reimagining master data as the foundation for enterprise AI

Why Attend

AI agents grounded in inconsistent or ungoverned master data produce unreliable outcomes — this session reframes MDM as the strategic prerequisite for trusted AI at scale. See how SAP Business Data Cloud unifies, governs, and delivers master data as reusable products that ground analytics, autonomous applications, and AI agents in consistent, trustworthy business context.

Key Takeaways

  • Structured master data products keep agents grounded in consistent, authoritative context — eliminating the inconsistency that causes unreliable or contradictory outputs in production.
  • Data stewards now hold a critical AI risk role — the governance rules, quality thresholds, and semantic metadata they define directly determine agent accuracy and auditability.
  • Master data quality is a strategic AI enabler, not just an operational concern — organizations investing in governed master data through SAP Business Data Cloud will deploy reliable, scalable agentic AI ahead of those that do not.

 

Data Engineers

DA100 | Enhancing agentic AI with trusted business data 

DA100V | Enhancing agentic AI with trusted business data (virtual)

Why Attend

This session answers a critical enterprise AI question: how do you ensure agents access accurate, governed, and contextually rich business data? Learn how SAP Business Data Cloud’s zero-copy architecture enables AI agents to consume trusted enterprise data in place — reducing data movement while maintaining the security, compliance, and control production AI demands.

Key Takeaways

  • Zero-copy architecture gives AI agents in-place access to enterprise data — eliminating movement and duplication while keeping governance controls fully intact.
  • Data product-level governance ensures context, permissions, and semantic meaning travel with the data — making agent outputs trustworthy and auditable by design, not retrospective monitoring.
  • Together, zero-copy access and data product-level governance shift AI quality assurance from reactive to proactive — giving architects a scalable, compliance-ready foundation for deploying agents with confidence.

 

DA200 | Agentic SAP BW modernization: Your path to SAP Business Data Cloud

Why Attend

If your organization is still running SAP BW and evaluating modernization, this session delivers the most current practical guidance available — including how AI agents now accelerate the migration journey. Explore proven strategies and dedicated tools that simplify the move to SAP Business Data Cloud while maximizing the value of your existing BW investments.

Key Takeaways

  • Dedicated migration tools and AI agents now automate large portions of the SAP BW modernization journey — reducing manual effort and resource demands while maximizing existing investments.
  • Modernizing to SAP Business Data Cloud isn’t starting over — existing BW models, hierarchies, and business logic are repositioned in a governed, AI-ready data fabric as the foundation for agentic AI, analytics, and planning.
  • Moving to SAP Business Data Cloud is both a technical migration and a strategic upgrade — organizations that modernize now gain a governed, purpose-built agentic AI platform ahead of those still constrained by legacy BW.

 

CT1163 | Under the hood of the Delta Sharing protocol

Why Attend

Zero-copy data sharing is the architectural standard for AI-ready data ecosystems — this technical session gives data engineers the depth to understand and implement the open-source Delta Sharing protocol across cloud and hybrid environments. See how a Delta Sharing server delivers live Delta tables from S3-compatible storage directly to consumers like Databricks — no data movement, no duplication, and governance built in.

Key Takeaways

  • Delta Sharing delivers a zero-copy architecture — live Delta tables stream from S3-compatible storage directly to cloud consumers like Databricks with no duplication, governance and access controls intact.
  • A Delta Sharing server gives engineers practical knowledge to ingest, govern, and operationalize live data sharing between hybrid storage and cloud-native analytics and AI platforms.
  • Together, zero-copy sharing and open standards eliminate two persistent barriers — data movement and proprietary lock-in — giving engineers a replicable, vendor-neutral pattern for connecting distributed data to AI and analytics workloads at scale.

 

Data Analysts

DA105 | Enriching AI models with SAP AI Core in SAP Business Data Cloud

Why Attend

AI models are only as powerful as their business context — this deep dive shows data scientists and practitioners how SAP AI Core integrates with SAP Business Data Cloud to enable semantically enriched, enterprise-grade AI. Learn how to enhance models with rich data products from SAP Business Data Cloud, supporting benchmarking, custom AI development, agentic analytics, and production-ready applications.

Key Takeaways

  • SAP Business Data Cloud data products enrich AI models with business-specific terminology, entity relationships, and domain context — delivering accurate, enterprise-relevant outputs without the overhead of extensive custom training.
  • The session delivers a practical, end-to-end path from governed data to production AI — a clear, repeatable technical approach for agentic analytics practitioners can apply immediately.
  • SAP Business Data Cloud and SAP AI Core carry semantic richness and governance from data products directly into AI model development — closing the gap between trusted enterprise data and reliable, auditable AI outcomes at scale.

 

DA260 | Accelerate agentic planning with trusted data products (hands-on workshop)

Why Attend

The most practical TechEd 2026 session for SAP planning professionals — a 2-hour workshop where you actually build agentic planning workflows, not just hear about them. Work directly with governed data products in SAP Business Data Cloud and SAP Analytics Cloud, learning how agentic AI automates planning tasks, generates insights, and drives faster, more informed decisions.

Key Takeaways

  • SAP Business Data Cloud data products anchor agentic planning to trusted, auditable data — enabling AI agents to automate planning tasks at scale while keeping governance and accountability intact.
  • The hands-on format builds direct SAP Analytics Cloud and SAP Business Data Cloud integration experience — creating business-ready data products and configuring AI workflows that automate repeatable planning activities.
  • Participants leave with end-to-end agentic planning knowledge — from governed data product creation in SAP Business Data Cloud to AI-automated insights and decision support in SAP Analytics Cloud — ready to apply immediately.

 

DA806 | What’s next for agentic analytics and planning in SAP Business Data Cloud

DA806V | What’s next for agentic analytics and planning in SAP Business Data Cloud (virtual)

Why Attend

For SAP Analytics Cloud analysts and planning professionals, this session maps where agentic analytics is heading — what's available now and what's coming — so you can align your strategy ahead of the curve. Discover how Joule Agents are already automating insight delivery, narrative generation, and modeling tasks within SAP Business Data Cloud, transforming analytics and planning into AI-enabled decision engines.

Key Takeaways

  • Joule Agents already automate core analytics workflows — insight delivery, data modeling, and narrative generation — freeing analysts to shift from routine report production to higher-value interpretation and decision support.
  • The session's forward-looking SAP Business Data Cloud roadmap gives practitioners the context to prioritize investments, align architectures, and plan skills development ahead of the curve.
  • Together, today's live capabilities and tomorrow's roadmap give data professionals a complete picture — what to adopt now for immediate productivity gains, and what to prepare for as Joule Agents scale.

 

Data Scientists

ST103 | Behind the Autonomous Enterprise: SAP Knowledge Graph and SAP Domain Models

ST103V | Behind the Autonomous Enterprise: SAP Knowledge Graph and SAP Domain Models (virtual)

Why Attend

This session reveals the intelligence architecture behind SAP’s Autonomous Enterprise vision — showing data scientists and architects how SAP Knowledge Graph, Domain Models, and tabular AI combine to deliver enterprise AI that reasons rather than merely predict. Learn what sets SAP Business AI Platform apart: a unified foundation where enterprise context, SAP-native expertise, and predictive capabilities converge within SAP AI Core for trustworthy, explainable outcomes.

Key Takeaways

  • SAP Knowledge Graph provides enterprise context — business semantics, hierarchies, and process knowledge — enabling AI to reason about actual operations rather than produce generic statistical outputs.
  • SAP Domain Models encode SAP-specific processes, code, and metadata into immediately applicable AI capabilities, while SAP-RPT-1 delivers accurate tabular predictions without training — giving SAP organizations a significant and immediate productivity advantage.
  • Together, SAP Knowledge Graph, Domain Models, and tabular AI form a unified intelligence foundation in SAP AI Core — closing the gap between raw AI potential and trustworthy, enterprise-grade reasoning data scientists and architects can build on with confidence.

 

RA803 | SAP Knowledge Graph, AI models, and AI core power SAP Business AI Platform

Why Attend

This session connects SAP's core AI infrastructure — Knowledge Graph, Domain Models, and AI Core — giving data scientists and architects a clear picture of what's production-ready and what's on the SAP Autonomous Suite roadmap. Learn how these technologies form the intelligence foundation for Joule-embedded, context-aware enterprise applications at scale, and leave with the context to align your AI architecture decisions with SAP's direction.

Key Takeaways

  • SAP Knowledge Graph, Domain Models, and AI Core form an integrated intelligence layer — the Graph delivers enterprise context, Domain Models contribute SAP-native expertise, and AI Core provides the infrastructure to orchestrate and govern AI workloads at scale.
  • The session delivers SAP's roadmap for these technologies and their expanding role in the SAP Autonomous Suite — giving practitioners the context to understand how today's architecture choices position organizations for automated, AI-driven operations.
  • Data scientists and architects who understand this intelligence layer gain a strategic advantage — designing AI architectures aligned with SAP's direction, reducing future rework and accelerating the path to Joule-embedded enterprise applications at scale.

 

DA204 | Unlock predictive and generative AI with your data in SAP HANA Cloud

DA204V | Unlock predictive and generative AI with your data in SAP HANA Cloud (virtual)

Why Attend

SAP HANA Cloud is evolving into a multi-model AI engine — combining tabular AI, a vector engine, and a knowledge graph to power both predictive and generative AI directly on live enterprise data. Discover the latest innovations including SQL-to-LLM capabilities and deep business context for GenAI, and leave knowing how to maximize your SAP HANA investment for production-ready AI.

Key Takeaways

  • SAP HANA Cloud's tabular AI and forecasting libraries deploy predictive models directly within the database — eliminating external ML platforms and enabling faster inference on live SAP transactional and analytical data.
  • The vector and knowledge graph engines enable RAG and context-aware GenAI directly on live enterprise data via SQL-to-LLM — removing the need for separate vector store infrastructure while keeping AI grounded in authoritative SAP data.
  • Together, tabular AI, vector search, and knowledge graph capabilities within a single SAP HANA Cloud engine give data scientists a unified, production-ready infrastructure — eliminating the complexity and data movement risk of managing multiple specialized platforms.

entry.title: GeoTrack: tracking trips in SAP HANA Cloud
entry.content:
GeoTrack is a portfolio project with exactly one user: me.

  • My iPhone records where I go.
  • My Apple Watch records my walks and hikes, and I pick the photos I want to keep.
  • Everything lands in SAP HANA Cloud.
  • Its spatial engine, which lets SQL store and measure points, lines and areas, turns raw positions into zones, trips and routes.
  • A RAP business object on an ABAP system records my visits to selected places.
  • A Fiori Elements app shows each trip with its route on a map, my heart rate, the altitude profile, the photos and the weather of every hour.
  • Claude, Anthropic's AI model, can answer questions about my trips through MCP tools.

I did not write GeoTrack's code. I decided what it should do and approved each design, and Claude wrote the code and the tests in Claude Code, from the HANA model and the RAP object to the Fiori app and the iOS app. I ran it on my own server and phone and checked the results.

This post walks through both versions of the architecture, explains why I asked Claude to replace two off-the-shelf senders with one iOS app, and shows the HANA spatial SQL that does the actual work.

The coordinates in the SQL examples are made up. The screenshots show real trips.

 

What GeoTrack does

  • Positions. Every position from the phone is stored as an ST_POINT in HANA Cloud, also while the trial database sleeps at night.
  • Zones. Places such as home, the supermarket or a trailhead are circles or polygons. A position inside a private zone is coarsened to the zone's centre before it is written.
  • Trips. Positions are cut into walks and drives using the iOS motion activity, and each route is stored as a LINESTRING.
  • Visits. A confirmed stay in a selected zone becomes a SiteVisit, a RAP business object on an ABAP Platform trial system.
  • Weather. Every closed trip gets the hourly weather from Open-Meteo.
  • Workouts and photos. Apple Watch workouts (always hikes - I live in the mountains), with heart rate and GPS route, and my photos are linked to the trips they belong to.
  • Apps. A read-only Fiori Elements List Report and Object Page shows all of it, and MCP tools let Claude answer questions about it.

 

Version 1: three senders

The first version used the best existing app for each job.

Positions came from OwnTracks. In Move mode it publishes a position when I have moved 50 m or when 300 seconds have passed. It sent JSON over MQTT to a Mosquitto broker on my VPS. The CAP service subscribed and acknowledged a message only after HANA had committed it.

Workouts came from Health Auto Export. Its REST automation posted my Apple Watch workouts, with heart rate samples and the GPS route, to an endpoint of the CAP service. It synced about once an hour after I unlocked the phone.

Photos came through my Mac. I AirDropped the photos of a walk to the Mac and dragged them into an inbox folder. A launchd agent read their metadata, made a small thumbnail without metadata and posted it.

The MQTT path had one property I liked a lot. The HANA Cloud trial stops every night. While it slept, the broker kept the phone's messages, and the CAP service received them again once HANA was back. Nothing was lost, only delayed.

 

Why I asked Claude to build my own iOS app

Version 1 worked. It also had three setups, three ways to fail and a Mac in the loop. These are the reasons I decided to replace it.

  • One app instead of three channels. Version 1 meant a broker to run and secure, a paid app's automation, and photos that arrived only when my Mac was awake and I remembered to drag them. Now one app talks HTTPS to one server.
  • More evidence on every position. The server decides which positions to trust, so it needs evidence. The app sends more data: the fields OwnTracks sent, plus the speed accuracy, the course accuracy and how confident iOS is about the motion activity. The difference showed early in the side-by-side run. During a 15-minute stop at a shop, OwnTracks delivered four positions inside the shop's zone, none of them classified as walking, so the server could not confirm the visit. The app delivered fourteen, with walking detected within two minutes of arrival.
  • Control over the recorder. The app has three modes: Auto, Manual (it records, but sends only when I tap) and Paused. A status screen shows what is waiting and why an upload stopped.
  • No junk at night. One night the database recorded a one-kilometre drive while I was asleep. An offline phone indoors had reported positions at motorway speed. The server now ignores positions outside zones based on vertical accuracy. The app also goes to sleep at home. When the phone has had no network for a minute (airplane mode, my habit at night) and its last fix lay inside the home zone, the app switches location updates off. iOS region monitoring wakes it if I leave the zone, and the network wakes it in the morning. A position that is never recorded needs no filter, and a GPS that is off uses no battery.
  • No subscription. Health Auto Export's REST automation belongs to its paid tier. My own app needs only the Apple Developer membership I already have.

The status screen, from the iOS Simulator with synthetic data. Left: everything is sent. Right: the server rejects the token, so seven positions wait on the phone.

How the app is built

A thin recorder. The phone records, queues and uploads. Zones, privacy rules and trips stay on the server, where they can be rebuilt from the raw data at any time. The phone drops only what iOS itself marks as invalid. It keeps the rhythm OwnTracks had, one position every 50 m or 300 seconds.

The contracts of the apps it replaced. Positions go to a new POST /positions route in OwnTracks' JSON shape. Workouts use Health Auto Export's JSON shape, and photos the shape the Mac agent used. The server's zone lookup, coarsening and trip rules did not change.

A queue on the phone instead of a broker. Every kept position is first written to the phone as a small file. Batches of up to 50 go to the server, and a batch leaves the phone only when the server's answer accounts for every position in it. While HANA sleeps, the server answers 503 and the app tries again a minute later. The server stores a position once per device and timestamp, so a resend does no harm.

Apple's frameworks only. Claude wrote the app with SwiftUI, Core Location, Core Motion, HealthKit and the iOS photo picker, without third-party packages. The logic (the keep rule, the queues, the uploaders, the workout sync and the photo metadata) lives in a Swift package with 202 tests that run on the Mac. Photos are picked in the app, so it never needs access to the whole library. It sends an 800 px thumbnail with all metadata removed, and the original never leaves the phone.

The app is currently waiting for review in the iOS App Store and hopefully will be approved soon.

 

Architecture today

From the phone to the server. The app posts to three routes, /positions, /health/workouts and /photos, through Caddy with TLS and a bearer token. Each answer to /positions also names the home zone as a circle, which is how the app knows where it may sleep. The first position after a sleep carries OwnTracks' region trigger, and the server starts the next trip there, from home, instead of treating the quiet night as a gap in the data.

CAP on a VPS, HANA Cloud on SAP BTP. The application layer is one CAP service (Node.js) in a Docker container on a small Linux VPS, next to Caddy and an ABAP Platform trial system. Only the database lives on SAP BTP, as an HDI container on a HANA Cloud trial instance. The VPS already ran Docker, Caddy and the ABAP trial, so one more container there was simpler than a second platform. The price is real: no XSUAA, no Destination service, no App Router. For a project with one user that trade is fine. With a second user, XSUAA would come first.

Inside the CAP service.

  • The ingest parses each position, asks HANA for its zone, coarsens it inside a private zone and inserts it.
  • The segmenter is a pure function that walks a device's positions in time order and produces zone events and trips. It uses the motion activity, rules for stops and silences, and accuracy limits that differ inside and outside zones. A runner calls it ten seconds after new data arrives and sweeps every five minutes.
  • Each closed trip gets hourly weather from Open-Meteo, with the coordinates rounded to about 1 km.
  • A confirmed stay in a flagged zone goes into CAP's persistent outbox, which delivers it to the ABAP system.

RAP on ABAP Platform. SiteVisit is a managed RAP business object with a bound close action and ABAP Unit tests for its validations, published as an OData V4 Web API. CAP consumes it as a remote service. The visit's key is a UUID v5 derived from the zone event, so a repeated create or close does no harm, and the outbox keeps retrying for about 14 hours while the ABAP system is down.

Fiori Elements. The trips app is a read-only List Report and Object Page on a CAP OData V4 service, built with SAPUI5 1.152 and driven mostly by annotations. Custom sections add the route map (a sap.ui.vbm GeoMap with OpenStreetMap tiles), the heart rate and altitude/speed charts (sap.viz, with the value of each point on hover) and the photos. Caddy publishes the app behind a password.

The screenshots show real trips: a drive with its route (at the top of the article), and a hike recorded by the Apple Watch, with its heart rate, altitude and photos.

 

 

The stop at the end of the drive became a SiteVisit on the ABAP system. My walk inside the shop confirmed the stay, CAP created the visit, and the bound close action recorded the departure when I drove off nine minutes later. This is the record as the OData V4 Web API returns it (trimmed, times in UTC):

{
  "VisitUUID": "c401443f-6e02-5a7e-87e8-9084f477e218",
  "ZoneName": "Supermarket",
  "Device": "iphone",
  "ArrivedAt": "2026-09-23T17:08:37Z",
  "DepartedAt": "2026-09-23T17:17:51Z",
  "Duration": 9.233,
  "DurationUnit": "MIN",
  "Status": "C",
  "ExtEventKey": "iphone|1408ffba-…|enter|2026-09-23T17:08:37.000Z"
}

 

MCP tools. A curated, read-only CAP service, exposed through @cap-js/mcp, lets Claude on my Mac answer questions like "How far did I walk this month, compared with last month?" or "Was it raining on any of my walks?". The tools (totals, zoneStats, tripsNear, tripDetail and a generic query) return times, lengths and distances, never coordinates.

 

HANA spatial, with examples

What HANA spatial is

SAP HANA has a spatial engine built in. Besides numbers, text and dates, a column can hold a geometry: a point, a line or an area. SQL can then answer geometric questions, such as how far apart two points are, whether a point lies inside an area, or which routes passed near a place. In SAP HANA Cloud it is part of the database, including the free trial, so there is nothing to install and no separate GIS server to run.

Four ideas are enough to read the examples below.

  • Geometry types. ST_POINT holds a single point. ST_GEOMETRY holds any shape, for example a POLYGON for an area or a LINESTRING for a route.
  • A spatial reference system. Every geometry carries an SRID, a number that says what its coordinates mean. GeoTrack uses SRID 4326, which is WGS 84, the latitude and longitude that GPS delivers. HANA treats 4326 as a round-earth system: distances follow the curve of the earth and can come back in metres rather than degrees.
  • Well-known text (WKT). A readable notation for shapes, such as POINT (1.5034 42.5021). ST_GeomFromText turns WKT into a geometry, and ST_AsText turns a geometry back into WKT. The x coordinate comes first, so the longitude comes before the latitude.
  • ST_ functions. Their names follow the SQL/MM and OGC Simple Features standards, so most of them match PostGIS. HANA calls most of them as methods of a geometry: where PostGIS writes ST_Distance(a, b), HANA writes a.ST_Distance(b). A new point is written NEW ST_POINT(1.5034, 42.5021, 4326).

You can try all four in any HANA Cloud SQL console, without creating a table. This query makes up a park, a home inside it and a shop outside it:

WITH PLACES AS (
  SELECT ST_GeomFromText(
           'POLYGON((1.50 42.50, 1.51 42.50, 1.51 42.51, 1.50 42.51, 1.50 42.50))',
           4326) AS PARK,
         NEW ST_POINT(1.5034, 42.5021, 4326) AS HOME,
         NEW ST_POINT(1.5130, 42.5064, 4326) AS SHOP
    FROM DUMMY)
SELECT ROUND(HOME.ST_Distance(SHOP, 'meter')) AS METRES,
       PARK.ST_Intersects(HOME) AS HOME_IN_PARK,
       PARK.ST_Intersects(SHOP) AS SHOP_IN_PARK,
       HOME.ST_AsText() AS HOME_WKT
  FROM PLACES;
-- METRES  HOME_IN_PARK  SHOP_IN_PARK  HOME_WKT
-- 922     1             0             POINT (1.5034 42.5021)

The home is 922 m from the shop, ST_Intersects answers 1 for the home and 0 for the shop, and the WKT puts the longitude first. In SRID 1000004326, SAP's planar version of WGS 84, the same HOME.ST_Distance(SHOP) returns 0.0105, in degrees.

GeoTrack needs only a handful of these functions: ST_Intersects to find a position's zone, ST_Distance for lengths and nearness, and WKT in both directions. HANA offers much more, from GeoJSON output to spatial clustering.

Doing this in the database keeps the work next to the data. Positions, zones and trips sit in ordinary tables, so one SQL statement can join them, filter by time and measure distances, instead of loading thousands of rows into application code.

In CAP, spatial columns use the types hana.ST_POINT and hana.ST_GEOMETRY. CAP does not write spatial values for you, so every spatial write in GeoTrack is native SQL through cds.db.run. Six patterns cover the whole project.

1. A point for every position

entity Positions {
  key device : String(40);
  key ts     : Timestamp;
      lat    : Decimal(9,6) not null;
      lon    : Decimal(9,6) not null;
  /** Position as ST_POINT, SRID 4326; set via native SQL on insert */
      point  : hana.ST_POINT(4326);
      // accuracy, altitude, speed, motion activity, zone, raw JSON, ...
}
INSERT INTO GEOTRACK_POSITIONS (DEVICE, TS, LAT, LON, POINT /* , ... */)
VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, NEW ST_POINT(?, ?, 4326) /* , ... */);
-- the point's parameters are (1.5034, 42.5021): longitude first

The first gotcha of the project: ST_POINT(x, y) takes the longitude first. The table keeps latitude and longitude as plain decimals as well, so the OData services and the Fiori app never touch the geometry type. In the SQL console the points read like this:

SELECT DEVICE, TS, POINT.ST_AsText() AS WKT
  FROM GEOTRACK_POSITIONS
 ORDER BY TS DESC;
-- POINT (1.5034 42.5021)

2. Which zone is this position in?

A zone is a circle or a polygon, and both live in one geometry column. For a circle, the service computes a 32-point polygon from the centre and the radius, and HANA parses the WKT. Here is a 200 m circle:

UPDATE GEOTRACK_ZONES SET GEOM = ST_GeomFromText(?, 4326) WHERE ID = ?;
-- 'POLYGON((1.5034 42.5039, 1.5038 42.5039, 1.5042 42.5038, ..., 1.5034 42.5039))'

Every incoming position asks HANA for its zone before it is inserted:

SELECT TOP 1 ID, ISPRIVATE, ISBASE, CENTRELAT, CENTRELON
  FROM GEOTRACK_ZONES
 WHERE GEOM IS NOT NULL
   AND GEOM.ST_Intersects(NEW ST_POINT(?, ?, 4326)) = 1
 ORDER BY ISPRIVATE DESC,
          CASE WHEN KIND = 'polygon' THEN 0 ELSE RADIUSM END ASC;

Zones overlap, so the ORDER BY decides. A private zone beats a public one, a polygon beats any circle, and among circles the smallest wins. When the winner is private, the position is written with the zone's centre instead of its own coordinates, and its raw JSON loses the coordinates and the Wi-Fi network's name and address. The real values are never stored.

3. A trip's length and line in one statement

When the segmenter closes a trip that only the phone recorded, HANA measures it (simplified): 

SELECT
  (SELECT ROUND(SUM(D)) FROM (
      SELECT POINT.ST_Distance(LAG(POINT) OVER (ORDER BY TS), 'meter') AS D
        FROM GEOTRACK_POSITIONS WHERE TRIP_ID = ?)) AS LENGTH_M,
  (SELECT 'LINESTRING(' || STRING_AGG(LON || ' ' || LAT, ', ' ORDER BY TS) || ')'
     FROM GEOTRACK_POSITIONS WHERE TRIP_ID = ?) AS ROUTE_WKT
FROM DUMMY;

UPDATE GEOTRACK_TRIPS SET ROUTE = ST_GeomFromText(ROUTEWKT, 4326) WHERE ID = ?;

 ST_Distance with LAG over the time order measures every step in metres, and the outer SUM adds up the path in one pass. STRING_AGG ... ORDER BY builds the WKT that becomes the LINESTRING and also the line the Fiori map draws. When the Apple Watch recorded a route during the trip, its denser points take over from the phone's for that stretch. That stitching runs in JavaScript, and every trip records whether its length came from the phone, the Watch or both.

4. Which trips passed near a place?

This query sits behind the MCP tool tripsNear. For every trip in a date range, it finds the position closest to a given point and keeps the trips that came within the radius (trimmed):

SELECT ID, STARTEDAT, KIND, LENGTHM, TS, D FROM (
  SELECT T.ID, T.STARTEDAT, T.KIND, T.LENGTHM, P.TS,
         P.POINT.ST_Distance(NEW ST_POINT(?, ?, 4326), 'meter') AS D,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY T.ID
           ORDER BY P.POINT.ST_Distance(NEW ST_POINT(?, ?, 4326), 'meter'), P.TS) AS RN
    FROM GEOTRACK_POSITIONS P
    JOIN GEOTRACK_TRIPS T ON T.ID = P.TRIP_ID
   WHERE T.ENDEDAT IS NOT NULL AND T.STARTEDAT >= ? AND T.STARTEDAT < ?)
 WHERE RN = 1 AND D <= ?
 ORDER BY D;

 A point goes in, and distances and times come out. When I ask about a place by name, Claude supplies its coordinates, calls the tool and answers with times and distances, without seeing a single one of my positions.

5. A set-based backfill instead of a correlated TOP 1

Zones came after the first positions, so every stored position needed its best zone. Claude's first attempt was a correlated subquery with TOP 1 ... ORDER BY, which HANA rejects. A MERGE over a ROW_NUMBER ranking does the same job in one statement, with the same precedence as the live lookup:

MERGE INTO GEOTRACK_POSITIONS P USING (
  SELECT DEVICE, TS, ID FROM (
    SELECT P.DEVICE, P.TS, Z.ID,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY P.DEVICE, P.TS
             ORDER BY Z.ISPRIVATE DESC,
                      CASE WHEN Z.KIND = 'polygon' THEN 0 ELSE Z.RADIUSM END) AS RN
      FROM GEOTRACK_POSITIONS P
      JOIN GEOTRACK_ZONES Z
        ON Z.GEOM IS NOT NULL AND P.POINT.ST_Intersects(Z.GEOM) = 1
     WHERE P.ZONE_ID IS NULL)
   WHERE RN = 1) S
ON P.DEVICE = S.DEVICE AND P.TS = S.TS
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET ZONE_ID = S.ID;

6. Thousands of points in one round trip

Positions are stored one per database round trip, about five per second when Claude measured it, which is plenty for batches of 50. A two-hour workout from the Watch can bring more than 7,000 route points. The workout route therefore inserts its rows without geometry and builds every point in one statement:

UPDATE GEOTRACK_WORKOUTROUTE
   SET POINT = NEW ST_POINT(TO_DOUBLE(LON), TO_DOUBLE(LAT), 4326)
 WHERE WORKOUT_ID = ?;

A workout of that size is stored in about five seconds. The private-zone check for its points runs in JavaScript against the zone polygons, which the service reads once per workout with GEOM.ST_AsWKT(), instead of making 7,000 ST_Intersects round trips.

HANA lessons in one list

  • ST_POINT(x, y) is (longitude, latitude).
  • No TOP or ORDER BY in a correlated subquery. Rank with ROW_NUMBER() and apply with MERGE.
  • In native SQL, BOOLEAN columns want the literals TRUE and FALSE, not 1 and 0.
  • AT is a reserved word, so a column named at must be quoted everywhere.
  • Timestamps come back without an offset. Parse them as UTC explicitly instead of letting JavaScript guess.
  • A trial instance stops every night. Design every writer for it.

 

Privacy by design

This is real personal data, so privacy lives in the write path.

  • Coarsening happens before the insert. Real coordinates inside a private zone are never written, and neither are the Wi-Fi network's name and hardware address (a BSSID can be geolocated through public databases).
  • Watch route points inside a private zone are coarsened the same way, and a photo taken inside one is not stored at all.
  • Photos travel as 800 px thumbnails without metadata, stripped on the phone and again on the server.
  • Open-Meteo receives one coordinate per trip hour, rounded to about 1 km.
  • The MCP tools never return coordinates.
  • The repository contains no real data. The tests use synthetic coordinates.

 

What I would tell someone starting a similar project

  • Keep the rules on the server. When the senders changed, HANA and the segmenter stayed as they were.
  • Copy the contract of the tool you replace. Then run old and new side by side under different device names and compare.
  • Let HANA do the geometry, set-based. One statement over many rows beats a round trip per row.
  • Design for the database being away. A queue on the phone, idempotent writes and retries that span a night turn the nightly stop into a non-event.
  • Expect surprises in photo metadata. iOS's ImageIO does not expose the time-zone offset of a ProRAW photo. The app reads the EXIF data itself, and for an edited ProRAW photo it derives the offset from the photo's GPS time.

 

By the numbers

  • First commit on 22 September 2026. The app took over from the three senders on 6 October 2026.
  • 282 commits, 279 of them co-authored by Claude.
  • 12 tables and 29 views in one HDI container on a shared HANA Cloud trial instance: the data model's 11 entities and 6 views, a table for CAP's persistent queue, and a view for each of the 23 entities the services expose.

  • 347 JavaScript tests and 202 Swift tests. None of them needs HANA.
  • 1 RAP business object with a bound action, 1 Fiori Elements app and 1 iOS app with two screens.
  • 1 CAP service with 3 upload routes, OData V4 services for the Fiori app and the MCP tools, and an OData client for the ABAP system.

If you work with HANA Cloud spatial, run CAP outside Cloud Foundry, or build with Claude Code, I'd be glad to compare notes in the comments.

The free public repo (MIT license) 👉 https://github.com/Kamilkov/geotrack-location

entry.title: An End-to-End Travel Approval App with SAP CAP, HANA Cloud, and SAP Build Process Automation
entry.content:
Goal

The goal is to build a working Travel Approval application, not just a collection of disconnected demos. A user creates a travel request in a Fiori Elements application. The CAP service stores the request in SAP HANA Cloud and automatically starts an SAP Build Process Automation workflow.

The approver reviews the task in My Inbox and selects Approve or Reject, updating the corresponding Travel record in HANA Cloud.

Create Travel in Fiori
       ↓
CAP saves the active record in HANA Cloud
       ↓
CAP starts the BPA workflow automatically
       ↓
Approval task appears in SAP Build Lobby->My Inbox
       ↓
Approve → overall_status = A
Reject → overall_status = R
       ↓
Validate in Fiori, SAP Build->Monitoring, and HANA Database Explorer

Prerequisites

BTP Service / instance required
SAP Business Application Studio
SAP HANA Cloud
SAP Build Process Automation

The End-to-End Flow

  1. Create Travel entity in CDS.
  2. Expose the entity as a draft-enabled OData V4 service.
  3. Generate the Fiori Elements application.
  4. Bind the CAP project to the HANA HDI container.
  5. Build the MTA archive and deploy it to Cloud Foundry.
  6. Download the CAP metadata as an EDMX specification.
  7. Create SAP Build Actions from the EDMX and test the OData operations.
  8. Create the Travel Context, API trigger, Approval Form, and approval branches in BPA.
  9. Create a BPA service key and an API key with trigger execution permission.
  10. Add the CAP SAVE handler that starts the workflow automatically.
  11. Test from Fiori, process the task in My Inbox, monitor the instance in Build Lobby, and validate the final status in HANA.

1. Model the CDS Entity for the CAP OData V4 Service

The CDS entity is the source of truth for the Travel data. The technical UUID and the business Travel ID form the key used by the draft-enabled service and by the generated SAP Build Actions.

1.1.    Expose the Travel entity as a service

Create file srv/service.cds.

Why draft support matters: Fiori Elements creates and edits a draft first. The active Travel record is produced when the user activates or saves the draft. The CAP SAVE event is therefore the reliable point for starting the workflow.

2. Create the Fiori Elements App

Generate a List Report/Object Page application for CAPWFService.Travel. The list lets users create requests and review the current status. The Object Page captures the full Travel details.

 

Figure 1. Fiori List Report with Travel IDs in ascending order.

3. Connect to Cloud Foundry

3.1.    Cloud Foundry provides the runtime for the deployed CAP service. Log in from the BAS terminal and select the correct organization and dev space.

cf login
cf target

3.2.    Before testing SAP Build Actions, always confirm that the deployed CAP application is running:

cf start CAPWF-srv
cf app CAPWF-srv

3.3.    Expected status:

requested state: started
instances: 1/1
state: running

Important: When CAPWF-srv was stopped, every SAP Build Action returned 404 Requested route does not exist. Starting the application restored the Actions immediately.

4. Bind to a HANA Cloud HDI Container

An HDI container is an application-scoped database container. It gives the CAP application its own isolated schema inside the HANA Cloud database.

cds bind --to CAPWF-db
cds env get requires.db --profile hybrid

The hybrid profile must show the CAPWF-db instance. Start the local service against HANA:

pkill -f cds
cds watch --profile hybrid

Look for connect to db > hana and the expected HANA schema in the terminal output.

Lesson learned: The lowercase capwf-db and uppercase CAPWF-db were two separate service instances. Local Fiori and deployed BPA initially showed different record counts because they were connected to different HDI containers.

5. Generate the MTAR File

The Multi-Target Application archive packages the service, database deployer, security resources, destinations, and HTML5 content into one deployable unit.

mbt build

The archive is generated under: mta_archives/CAPWF_1.0.0.mtar

6. Deploy to HANA Cloud and Cloud Foundry

cf deploy mta_archives/CAPWF_1.0.0.mtar

The deployment runs the database deployer, binds CAPWF-srv to CAPWF-db and CAPWF-auth, and starts the application route.

cf app CAPWF-srv
cf routes
cf logs CAPWF-srv --recent

Free-tier note: Stopping applications frees runtime memory, but it also makes the CAP route unavailable. Start CAPWF-srv again before testing browser URLs or SAP Build Actions.

7. Connect to the HANA DB Explorer and Add the HDI Container

7.1.    Open SAP HANA Database Explorer.

7.2.    Choose Add Database or Add HDI Container.

7.3.    Select the CAPWF-db HDI container.

7.4.    Expand Catalog and Tables.

7.5.    Open the Travel table data and compare the record count with the Fiori app.

7.6.    After approval or rejection, refresh the table and verify overall_status.

Figure 2. CAPWF-db added to SAP HANA Database Explorer.

8. Download the Metadata File as EDMX

The metadata document describes the OData V4 service, entity fields, keys, draft properties, and custom actions. SAP Build uses this specification to generate reusable Actions.

/service/CAPWFService/$metadata

Open the metadata->right-click->Save as .edmx file

Open the local BAS port 4004 metadata URL, save the XML as CAPWFService.edmx, and verify that it contains:

  • EntitySet Name="Travel"
  • The Travel entity fields and keys
  • Draft operations
  • Action Name="submitForApproval" IsBound="true"

9. Create SAP Build Actions

9.1. Open SAP Build Lobby -> Actions -> Create.

9.2. Choose Upload API Specification.

9.3. Upload CAPWFService.edmx.

9.4. Create the Action project CAPWFService3.

9.5. Select the required Travel operations. The POC selected all 13 generated operations.

10.   Open Settings and configure the destination and URL prefix.

SettingValue
DestinationCAPWF-srv
URL Prefix/service/CAPWFService
CSRFDisabled for this POC
Destination authenticationOAuth2ClientCredentials

11.   Test the Actions before publishing

11.1.   Get entities from Travel should return 200 OK and all records. - see the image below

11.2.   Get entity from Travel by key should return the selected record using ID, travel_id, and  IsActiveEntity=true.

11.3.   Update entity in Travel should be validated independently before adding it to the process.

11.4.   Release and Publish only after direct tests succeed.

cf logs CAPWF-srv cf app CAPWF-srv cf start CAPWF-srv -->You can see the Instances are up and Running 1/14.       The root cause may simply be a stopped application.

Troubleshooting shortcut: If all Actions suddenly return 404 and no request reaches, run the below commands in new Terminal.

 

Figure 2. CAPWFService3 Action test returning 200 OK.

12. Steps in SAP Build Process Automation

12.1.Create the project and artifacts

12.2.Create the project RAP110_Travel_Workflow.

12.3.Create the process of Travel Approval Processing.

12.4.Create the Travel Context datatype.

12.5.Create a Travel Approval Trigger as an API trigger.

12.6.Create the Approval Form and map the Travel fields.

12.7.Add Approve and Reject outcomes.

12.8.Add Update entity in Travel from the published CAPWFService3 dependency.

12.9.Map the keys and set overall_status to A in Approve and R in Reject.

13. Travel Context fields

FieldData Type
TravelUUIDString
TravelIDNumber
IsActiveEntityBoolean
agency_idNumber
customer_idNumber
begin_dateDate
end_dateDate
booking_feeNumber
total_priceNumber
currency_codeString
descriptionString
overall_statusString

14. Approval Form recipient

When a human starts the workflow manually, Started By is the signed-in user. When CAP starts the process using client credentials, Started By is a technical client. For the POC, the Approval Form recipient was set to the intended email address, so the work item appeared in My Inbox. A production design should pass an ApproverEmail value or determine the approver through business rules.

15. Add and Delete Dependencies

15.1.A process can use only released and published Action projects through Dependencies.

15.2.Open the editable BPA project and switch to Dependencies.

15.3.Add the published CAPWFService3 Action project.

15.4.If an old Action dependency is removed, delete any orphaned process nodes that show blank Inputs.

15.5.Re-add the Actions from CAPWFService3 and remap their inputs.

15.6.To remove a dependency, select it, choose Settings, and select Delete.

15.7.If an Action project cannot be deleted, remove consuming dependencies and delete its released versions first.

16. Create an API Key in SAP Build

The CAP application starts the process as a technical client. It therefore needs both OAuth client credentials and an SAP Build API key that is authorized to execute the trigger.

16.1.Open SAP Build -> Control Tower -> API Keys, or Public Environment -> API Keys.

16.2.Choose Add API Key.

16.3.Enter a meaningful name, such as CAPWF_Auto_Start.

16.4.Select the Public environment.

16.5.Enable trigger_execute. This is the minimum scope needed to execute the API trigger.

16.6.Create the key and copy it immediately. The value is displayed only once.

17. Build Process Automation - Manual Workflow Test Using the Payload

Before automating the trigger from CAP, manually prove the deployed process and payload schema.

17.1.Open Control Tower -> Environments -> Public -> Triggers.

17.2.Open Travel Approval Trigger.

17.3.Choose Start New Instance.

17.4.Paste only the process context expected by the dialog, with travelContext as the root object.

17.5.Start the instance and confirm it appears in Monitoring.

17.6.Open My Inbox and process the task.

17.7.Confirm the instance completes and the Travel status is updated.

{
"travelContext": {
   "TravelUUID": "<UUID>",
   "TravelID": 15,
   "IsActiveEntity": true,
   "agency_id": 70015,
   "customer_id": 70015,
   "begin_date": "2026-10-02",
   "end_date": "2026-10-16",
   "booking_fee": 150,
   "total_price": 150,
   "currency_code": "INR",
   "description": "Travel request",
   "overall_status": "W"
}
}

18. List of Terminal Commands to Get BPA Keys

cf create-service-key BPA cap-bpa-key
cf service-key BPA cap-bpa-key

From the BPA service key, record these values securely: clientid, clientsecret, and URL. The token endpoint is the URL value plus /oauth/token.

Do not mix credentials: CAPWF-auth credentials protect the CAP application. BPA service-key credentials authenticate the call to SAP Build Process Automation. Using CAPWF-auth credentials caused 401 invalid_client / Bad credentials.

19. Start the Workflow Automatically from CAP

The Fiori application activates a draft when the user saves a new Travel. CAP handles that lifecycle through the SAVE event. The handler builds the exact trigger payload, obtains an OAuth token, sends the BPA API key, and creates the workflow instance.

// create a file in srv/service.js

this.after('SAVE', 'Travel', async (data, req) => {
   const travel = req.data;

   const workflowPayload = {
       definitionId:
         'us10.e66895ddtrial.rap110travelworkflow.travelApprovalProcessing',
       context: {
           travelContext: {
               TravelUUID: travel.ID,
               TravelID: travel.travel_id,
               IsActiveEntity: true,
               agency_id: travel.agency_id,
               customer_id: travel.customer_id,
               begin_date: travel.begin_date,
               end_date: travel.end_date,
               booking_fee: Number(travel.booking_fee),
               total_price: Number(travel.total_price),
               currency_code: travel.currency_code,
               description: travel.description,
               overall_status: travel.overall_status
           }
       }
   };

   // 1. Get an OAuth token with BPA client credentials.
   // 2. POST workflowPayload to BPA_WORKFLOW_URL.
   // 3. Send Authorization: Bearer <token> and api-key headers.
});

20. Verify in BAS with Three Terminals

20.1.   Terminal 1 - Run local CAP with BPA credentials

export BPA_CLIENT_ID='<BPA service-key clientid>'
export BPA_CLIENT_SECRET='<BPA service-key clientsecret>'
export BPA_TOKEN_URL='<BPA service-key url>/oauth/token'
export BPA_API_KEY='<SAP Build Public environment API key>'
export BPA_WORKFLOW_URL='https://spa-api-gateway-bpi-us-prod.cfapps.us10.hana.ondemand.com/workflow/rest/v1/workflow-instances'

pkill -f cds
cds watch --profile hybrid

20.2.   Terminal 2 - Confirm the deployed CAP app is running

cf start CAPWF-srv
cf app CAPWF-srv

20.3.   Terminal 3 - Watch deployed CAP requests

cf logs CAPWF-srv

A successful automatic start prints:

BPA workflow started for Travel 5
Workflow instance ID: <generated instance ID>

Session behavior: The export commands apply only to the current terminal session.

After BAS signs out or a new terminal is opened, export the variables again before cds watch.

21. Test Directly from the Fiori Application

21.1.Confirm Terminal 1 has BPA environment variables, and cds watch is running.

21.2.Confirm CAPWF-srv is 1/1 running if the workflow will call CAP through SAP Build Actions.

21.3.Open the Fiori Preview.

21.4.Create a new Travel record with overall_status W.

21.5.Save the record.

21.6.Watch Terminal 1 for the workflow instance ID.

21.7.Open SAP Build My Inbox and process the Travel task.

21.8.Refresh the Fiori List Report and confirm A or R.

22. My Inbox - Approve or Reject

The approver opens the Travel task, reviews the Travel fields, and chooses Approve or Reject. The process follows the corresponding branch and calls the CAP update Action. The completed workflow should disappear from My Inbox and appear as Completed in Monitoring.

If My Inbox is empty: Open the instance Logs. If the recipient is a technical client instead of the intended user, revise the Approval Form recipient mapping and deploy a new version.

23. Monitor Workflow Instances

23.1.Open SAP Build -> Monitoring -> Processes and Workflows.

23.2.Open Travel Approval Processing.

23.3.Filter by Running, Error, or Completed.

23.4.Open an instance and inspect Logs to see each executed step.

23.5.Open Context to confirm startEvent.travelContext values.

23.6.Use the instance ID printed by CAP to correlate the application request with the workflow instance.

Figure 4. Completed Travel Approval Processing instance.

24. Validate in the HDI Container

24.1.Open SAP HANA Database Explorer and refresh CAPWF-db.

24.2.Open the Travel table data.

24.3.Locate the Travel ID used in the test.

24.4.Confirm W before approval.

24.5.Confirm A after approval or R after rejection.

24.6.Compare the result with the Fiori List Report.

What Broke, Why It Broke, and the Fix

pkill -f cds​then start one runtime.

SymptomRoot causeFix
Fiori showed more records than BPA/HANADifferent HDI containers were usedBind local hybrid runtime to CAPWF-db.
Port 4004 already in useAn old cds process was still running 
Actions returned 404 route do not existCAPWF-srv was stoppedcf start CAPWF-srv and confirm 1/1 running.
Metadata returned UnauthorizedXSUAA was protecting the deployed serviceUse OAuth2ClientCredentials in CAPWF-srv destination.
BPA trigger returned invalid_clientCAPWF-auth credentials were used instead of BPA service-key credentialsUse cf service-key BPA cap-bpa-key values.
Workflow URL was Invalid URLEnvironment variables were missing after BAS re-loginExport variables in the same terminal before cds watch.
Workflow instance existed but My Inbox was emptyStarted By resolved to the technical OAuth clientUse an explicit recipient or dynamic ApproverEmail.
Action Inputs were blankProcess node referenced a removed Action dependencyDelete and re-add the node from the active dependency.
Travel ID sorting was inconsistentPresentation Variant did not reference the LineItem visualizationAdd Visualizations: ['@UI.LineItem'].
SAVE handler received data differently than CREATEFiori used draft activationUse after SAVE and req.data.

Conclusion

The solution combines Fiori Elements for data entry, CAP for service logic, HANA Cloud for persistence, and SAP Build Process Automation for approval. Success depends on aligning code, runtime state, destinations, credentials, recipients, dependencies, and HDI bindings. Once aligned, users can create, approve or reject, and view Travel requests in one application.

For similar integrations, test each connection independently: Fiori–CAP, CAP–HANA, CAP–BPA, BPA–CAP Actions, and task assignment. This turns a complex landscape into manageable checkpoints.

References

  • SAP Help: SAP Build Process Automation authorizations
  • SAP Help: SAP Business Application Studio roles
  • SAP Help: API Keys 
  • SAP Help: Execute an API Trigger
  • SAP Help: Use API Keys
  • SAP Help: Configure an API Trigger to Start a Process

entry.title: HighRadius vs. SAP FSCM: Hard-Earned Lessons from a Global Cosmetics S/4HANA Transformation
entry.content:
As consumer goods and beauty organizations accelerate their digital finance transformations, the debate surrounding Accounts Receivable (AR) optimization often gets reduced to a binary question: Should we use native SAP Financial Supply Chain Management (FSCM) or replace it with a specialized cloud solution like HighRadius? Over an 18-year career leading global SAP transformations across Europe, Asia, and the Middle East, I have watched finance executives repeatedly fall into the trap of treating this as an "either/or" software selection choice.

The reality on the ground is completely different. When you move past the product brochures and slide decks, you discover that the most successful global templates do not choose between them. Instead, they treat SAP as the core transactional engine and HighRadius as an intelligent edge layer. Achieving this coexistence, however, requires navigating complex architectural integration points, version-specific database behaviors, and industry-specific commercial nuances—such as complex trade promotions and massive retail deductions—that software vendors rarely mention during the sales cycle.

The Friction Point: Why Pure SAP FSCM Fell Short in Global Beauty & Cosmetics Rollouts

To understand where native capabilities hit their limits, we can look at a global cosmetics leader's rollout running on an SAP S/4HANA 2023 On-Premises environment with Feature Package Stack 02 (FPS02). The business model managed a deeply fragmented customer landscape: massive multinational retail networks (such as Sephora, Ulta, and major department stores), thousands of highly localized salon accounts, and high-volume e-commerce payment clearing.

Initially, the steering committee pushed for a pure SAP FSCM Collections and Dispute Management implementation to minimize their software footprint and leverage their existing licensing. However, as we entered the blueprinting and prototyping phases, the operational limitations of a purely rule-based system in the cosmetics industry became apparent:

  • The Trade Promotion Deduction Avalanche: Major retail beauty chains routinely short-pay invoices based on cooperative advertising agreements, volume rebates, and markdown allowances. In standard SAP FSCM, these deductions flood the subledger as individual residual open items. Dispute specialists spent up to 40% of their day manually linking these short payments to promotional agreements, creating a massive operational backlog.
  • Static Collection Strategies: SAP FSCM generates collection worklists based on static, pre-defined rules—such as aging buckets, risk categories, and total open values. In a fast-moving retail consumer landscape, these rigid rules created bottlenecks. The system flooded collection specialists with alerts for large, stable retail accounts that routinely paid according to strict corporate payment cycles, while high-risk, deteriorating independent salon behaviors slipped through unnoticed because they hadn't crossed a specific net-due threshold.
  • The Analytics Deficit: Standard SAP operational reporting (even via custom operational data provisioning views or standard Fiori FES 2023 apps) provided lagging operational KPIs. The business leadership lacked predictive cash forecasting and granular, dynamic Day Sales Outstanding (DSO) trend analysis segmented by shifting channel behavior patterns (D2C vs. B2B Wholesale).

The organization realized that while FSCM was perfectly engineered to maintain the financial integrity of the ledger, it lacked the algorithmic agility needed to optimize cash application hit rates and automatically resolve multi-brand deduction claims. This realization shifted our strategy to a hybrid architecture deploying the HighRadius Cash Application Cloud and Deduction Management System (DMS) modules alongside our SAP core.

Architectural Reality: Orchestrating Integration via Hyperion Integration Platform (HIP)

Integrating a multi-entity S/4HANA 2023 core with a cloud-based Autonomous Finance platform is rarely a "plug-and-play" exercise. For this transformation, we built a hybrid ecosystem where SAP functioned strictly as the immutable system of record, while HighRadius operated as the system of engagement and intelligence, orchestrated via the Hyperion Integration Platform (HIP) as the corporate middleware layer.

The underlying architecture relied on standardizing data exchange protocols across an enterprise footprint. Because the corporate landscape utilized HIP as its centralized enterprise middleware, we funneled all transactional deltas, ledger extract files, and incoming bank lockbox information through this layer to perform essential schema transformations before delivering them to High Radius.

The technical complexity surfaced heavily during the orchestration of the data loop between HighRadius Cash App, DMS, and SAP FI-AR via HIP:

  1. The Cash App Ingestion: HighRadius Cash App automatically extracts unstructured remittance data via OCR from customer emails and retail vendor portals, matching payments against open customer line items. This open item subledger data is periodically extracted from SAP operational views (such as BSID) and delivered through HIP as a structured outbound file payload.
  2. The DMS Splitting Mechanism: When a retail client short-pays an invoice due to a trade promotion dispute, the Cash App module flags the variance and automatically routes the residual shortage amount to the HighRadius DMS module.
  3. Automated Inbound Postings through HIP: Once a deduction is classified in the cloud, HighRadius communicates the clearing parameters back down. HIP intercepts this response payload, translates the cloud parameters into SAP-compatible structures, and executes an inbound transactional interface leveraging standard functions like BAPI_ACC_DOCUMENT_POST. This automatically clears the original invoice line item in S/4HANA, posts a residual open item for the short-payment, and maps specific SAP Reason Codes corresponding to the dispute type (e.g., Pricing, Shortage, or Coop Ad).

By utilizing HIP as the unified integration layer, we eliminated complex point-to-point interface sprawl, ensuring that our daily cash application cycle remained decoupled from the extended timelines required to research and settle retail trade promotions.

Version Constraints and Unexpected Implementation Roadblocks

Moving from conceptual architecture to actual deployment on S/4HANA 2023 (FPS02) exposed several technical constraints that project planners frequently overlook.

Our first major hurdle involved the Universal Journal (ACDOCA). In older SAP ERP Central Component (ECC) environments, financial data was highly segmented across index tables (like BSID and BSAD). S/4HANA’s unified ACDOCA design vastly speeds up internal reporting, but extracting massive delta datasets of open and cleared items to feed external machine learning models can degrade system performance if not carefully managed.

During initial data cycles, our delta extraction queries for historical customer payment behaviors began causing severe memory bottlenecks in the SAP HANA database due to the sheer volume of line items generated by cosmetic wholesale shipments. We had to configure the SAP extraction jobs and HIP to abandon generic open-ended queries and completely redesign our extraction logic. We restricted data pulls to strict timestamp-based delta captures leveraging specialized SAP Change Data Capture (CDC) mechanisms, ensuring that data replication to HighRadius occurred in controlled micro-batches outside of peak financial closing windows.

Another critical constraint appeared within the Business Partner (BP) master data synchronization. Because this was a global program spanning multiple geographies and brands, the client utilized complex BP groupings with varying field modification rules across different company codes. HighRadius requires a highly standardized payload for its ingestion models.

We encountered repeated integration errors where localized fields in SAP (such as specific regional tax classification rules or localized payment block reasons) caused data validation rejections in the HighRadius staging tables. This required a comprehensive data-cleansing initiative and configuring specialized transformation rules within HIP to map heterogeneous SAP BP attributes into a unified schema that the HighRadius machine learning algorithms could accurately interpret.

The Measurable Bottom Line: Concrete Project Outcomes

The true validation of this hybrid architectural strategy lies in the quantifiable business results achieved in 12 months of post-go-live. By shifting from static, rule-based workflows to an AI-driven, predictive model, the global shared services organization transformed its balance sheet performance:

 

The dramatic leap in our auto-cash application hit rate was particularly impactful for the consumer goods model. By leveraging HighRadius’s OCR and machine learning algorithms to automatically parse unstructured remittance advices from customer emails and retail vendor portals, the system matched payments to open items in S/4HANA without human intervention. This freed up our senior credit analysts to focus exclusively on negotiating complex promotional shortages rather than manual data entry.

Strategic Recommendations for Enterprise Architects Today

If I were to approach a global cosmetics architecture rollout again today, I would change my implementation strategy in two distinct areas:

  1. Mandate Early-Stage Data Cleansing: Do not wait for the integration testing phase to discover that your SAP Business Partner master data or customer hierarchies are inconsistent across regions. Master data remediation must be treated as a strict technical prerequisite that runs six months before any external cloud integration work begins.
  2. Enforce the Transactional Boundaries Immediately: Be incredibly disciplined about keeping business logic where it belongs. Cloud platforms will tempt you to build complex custom validation workflows or store trade promotion contracts within their environments. Resist this pressure. All accounting principles, credit limits, and final clearing rules must reside strictly within the S/4HANA core to protect your financial system of record. Use the HIP-enabled cloud edge purely for execution speed, prediction, and user experience.

Ultimately, the choice between SAP FSCM and HighRadius is a false dichotomy. The real challenge—and the real opportunity for enterprise architects—lies in configuring a robust, high-performing integration framework that respects the transactional authority of SAP while fully unleashing the analytical power of autonomous finance.

Author Bio

Prakashreddy Bodireddy is an SAP S/4HANA Certified FICO Solution Architect with 18+ years of experience delivering global finance transformation programs across Europe, the Middle East, Africa, Asia, and the Americas. His expertise includes SAP S/4HANA Finance, FSCM,  Group Reporting, IFRS15/RAR, Treasury, and HighRadius integration.
